topic: Price-data policy, the single gate that blocks most of the plan
options: A: adopt an official operator feed that the NFL publishes for partners; B: adopt a licensed commercial feed and store only derived, non-redistributable features; C: keep the price store empty and run the project as a pure forecasting desk with no staking or ROI claim.
recommended_path: C for now, with B as the target. The empty store is honest and already implemented, and the model can be judged on forecast quality alone until a feed is licensed. Choose B before any backtest with a money outcome is published.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a written, signed permission for a named feed with a quote timestamp, a jurisdiction and a push and void rule set. What would keep it: the model still cannot be scored on money without that document.

topic: Depth-order source for the Houston Texans
options: A: find an official structured source for the Texans depth page, for example a feed or a printable page rather than the image; B: use the official Game Book across a season to build actual-starter history and treat it as the depth proxy; C: keep Houston out of every depth-based feature and label it as missing.
recommended_path: B plus C now, A as the goal. The Game Book route is already proven on one game and it is the only official source that publishes who actually started, which is the quantity the feature actually needs.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: an official structured Texans source would remove the exception entirely. What would keep it: no such source appears on the club site, and the brief forbids transcription by eye.

topic: Whether the pre-registered shadow baseline should stay published
options: A: keep publishing it with the shadow label and the train, validation and holdout split visible on every row; B: withdraw all backtest numbers and publish only prospective scores; C: keep publishing it but add a second untouched holdout.
recommended_path: A now, C before any strategy is staked. The published numbers show exactly why the label matters: the validation week gave a Brier skill of 0.44 and the final holdout gave 0.02. Removing the numbers would hide that lesson.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a second holdout season that the model has never seen would let the number stand on its own. What would keep it: nothing in the numbers themselves changes; the label and the split do the work.

options: A: join designations to official inactive lists across three past seasons and estimate a play rate per designation; B: use the designation only as a filter, never as a weight; C: do not use designations at all until the archive exists.
recommended_path: A, with C as the interim. The archive of past weekly reports is a public, dated source, so the join is achievable; until then the designation is a filter and never a number in a model.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a season of joins that produces a tight interval on the Questionable play rate. What would keep it: wide intervals or a designation that predicts nothing.

topic: Two estimators for the model total, and when one may be retired
options: A: publish both estimators and their gap indefinitely; B: retire the weaker estimator after a chronological walk-forward comparison; C: replace both with a single point estimate and publish the interval instead.
recommended_path: B with A until then. The walk-forward rule must be written before the comparison is run, so that the retirement is not chosen after seeing which one wins.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a pre-written walk-forward rule that names the estimator, the window and the decision threshold before the run. What would keep it: the gap column stays until that rule has fired.

topic: Public analysis layer versus private data layer
options: A: publish everything including raw rows; B: publish only derived indices, ratios and model output, and link to the official page; C: publish nothing but links.
recommended_path: B. It is already the posture of this desk: derived analysis in public, and a link to the official page for every fact. It also removes the terms question from the critical path.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a written terms review that permits raw row-level republication. What would keep it: the review is not complete, so the conservative layer stays.

topic: The price store, the results feed and the standings: one canonical file or many
options: A: one canonical results feed with every desk reading it; B: keep the per-desk feeds and publish a reconciliation report; C: rebuild the feeds from the official pages on a schedule and drop the carried-forward rows.
recommended_path: C for the corpus, because a carried-forward row is only as good as the capture that produced it, and one stale row has already been found. Until the scheduled rebuild exists, B keeps the reconciliation visible.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a scheduled rebuild that reproduces the corpus from the official pages with 0 mismatches against the standings. What would keep it: the reconciliation report is the only thing that currently catches a stale row.

topic: What counts as a fair comparison for the removal-of-luck panel
options: A: compare against the climatology baseline only; B: compare against the climatology baseline and both controls, as this desk does; C: compare against a second independent model.
recommended_path: B. With three trials the Bonferroni-adjusted significance level is 0.0167, and a panel that shows only the model can hide a lucky run.
what_would_change_our_mind: What would change this: a second independently specified model whose forecasts are registered before the window opens. What would keep it: the controls are free, reproducible and already published.
